title: Chapter 91 — The Pequod Meets The Rose-Bud
paragraphs: "In vain it was to rake for Ambergris in the paunch of this Leviathan, insufferable stench denying not inquiry." — Sir T. Browne, V.E.

It was a week or two after the last whaling scene recounted, and when we were slowly sailing over a sleepy, hazy, midday sea, that the many noses on the Pequod's deck proved more vigilant discoverers than the three pairs of eyes aloft. A peculiar and not very pleasant smell was detected in the sea.
"I'll bet something now," said Stubb, "that somewhere nearby are some of those dragged whales we stabbed the other day. I thought they'd turn belly-up before long."

Presently, the haze ahead slid aside, and there in the distance lay a ship whose furled sails indicated that some sort of whale must be alongside. As we glided nearer, the stranger showed French colors from her peak. And by the eddying cloud of vulture sea-birds that circled, hovered, and swooped around her, it was plain that the whale alongside must be what the fishermen call a blasted whale — that is, a whale that has died unmolested on the sea and so floated as an unclaimed corpse. You can well imagine what an unsavory odor such a mass must give off — worse than an Assyrian city in the plague, when the living cannot bury the dead. So intolerable is it considered by some that no greed could persuade them to moor alongside it. Yet there are those who will still do it, notwithstanding the fact that the oil obtained from such subjects is of very inferior quality, and by no means of the nature of rose-water.

Coming still nearer with the dying breeze, we saw that the Frenchman had a second whale alongside. This second whale seemed even more of a stench-bouquet than the first. In truth, it turned out to be one of those problematical whales that seem to dry up and die with a sort of prodigious indigestion, leaving their dead bodies almost entirely bankrupt of anything like oil. Nevertheless, in the proper place we shall see that no knowledgeable fisherman will ever turn up his nose at such a whale as this, however much he may shun blasted whales in general.
The Pequod had now swept so close to the stranger that Stubb swore he recognized his cutting spade-pole entangled in the lines knotted around the tail of one of these whales.

"There's a pretty fellow now," he banteringly laughed, standing in the ship's bow. "There's a jackal for you! I well know that these Frenchmen are poor devils in the fishery — sometimes lowering their boats for breakers, mistaking them for sperm whale spouts. Yes, and sometimes sailing from their port with their hold full of tallow candles and cases of snuffers, foreseeing that all the oil they'll get won't be enough to dip the captain's wick into. Aye, we all know these things. But look here, here's a Frenchman that is content with our leavings — the dragged whale there, I mean. Aye, and content too with scraping the dry bones of that other precious fish he has there. Poor devil! Pass round a hat, someone, and let's make him a present of a little oil for dear charity's sake. For what oil he'll get from that dragged whale there wouldn't be fit to burn in a jail — no, not in a condemned cell. And as for the other whale, why, I'll agree to get more oil by chopping up and boiling out these three masts of ours than he'll get from that bundle of bones. Though, now that I think of it, it may contain something worth a good deal more than oil. Yes — ambergris. I wonder now if our old man has thought of that. It's worth trying. Yes, I'm for it." And so saying he started for the quarter-deck.

By this time the faint breeze had become a complete calm, so that like it or not, the Pequod was now fairly trapped in the smell, with no hope of escaping unless the wind picked up again. Coming out of the cabin, Stubb called his boat's crew and pulled off for the stranger. Drawing across her bow, he saw that in accordance with the fanciful French taste, the upper part of her stem-piece was carved in the likeness of a huge drooping stalk, was painted green, and for thorns had copper spikes projecting from it here and there — the whole terminating in a symmetrical folded bulb of a bright red color. Upon her headboards, in large gilt letters, he read "Bouton de Rose" — Rose-button, or Rose-bud. And this was the romantic name of this aromatic ship.
Though Stubb did not understand the "Bouton" part of the inscription, the word "rose" and the bulbous figurehead put together sufficiently explained the whole to him.
"A wooden rose-bud, eh?" he cried with his hand to his nose. "That will do very well. But how like all creation it smells!"
Now in order to communicate directly with the people on deck, he had to pull around the bow to the starboard side, and thus come close to the blasted whale and talk over it.
Arriving at this spot, with one hand still to his nose, he bawled: "Bouton-de-Rose, ahoy! Are there any of you Bouton-de-Roses that speak English?"
"Yes," replied a Guernseyman from the bulwarks, who turned out to be the chief mate.
"Well then, my Bouton-de-Rose-bud, have you seen the White Whale?"
"What whale?"
"The White Whale — a sperm whale — Moby Dick. Have you seen him?"
"Never heard of such a whale. Cachalot Blanche! White Whale — no."
"Very good, then. Goodbye now, and I'll call again in a minute."

Then rapidly pulling back toward the Pequod, and seeing Ahab leaning over the quarter-deck rail awaiting his report, he cupped his two hands into a trumpet and shouted: "No, sir! No!" Upon which Ahab retired, and Stubb returned to the Frenchman.
He now noticed that the Guernseyman, who had just gotten into the chains and was using a cutting-spade, had slung his nose in a sort of bag.
"What's the matter with your nose there?" said Stubb. "Broken it?"
"I wish it was broken, or that I didn't have any nose at all!" answered the Guernseyman, who did not seem to relish the job he was at very much. "But what are you holding yours for?"
"Oh, nothing! It's a wax nose — I have to hold it on. Fine day, isn't it? Air rather garden-like, I should say. Throw us a bunch of posies, will you, Bouton-de-Rose?"
"What in the devil's name do you want here?" roared the Guernseyman, flying into a sudden rage.

"Oh, keep cool — cool? Yes, that's the word! Why don't you pack those whales in ice while you're working at them? But joking aside, though — do you know, Rose-bud, that it's all nonsense trying to get any oil out of such whales? As for that dried-up one there, he hasn't a drop in his whole carcass."

"I know that well enough. But, d'you see, the Captain here won't believe it. This is his first voyage — he was a Cologne manufacturer before. But come aboard, and maybe he'll believe you, if he won't believe me. And so I'll get out of this dirty mess."

"Anything to oblige you, my sweet and pleasant fellow," replied Stubb, and with that he soon climbed onto the deck. There a queer scene presented itself. The sailors, in tasseled caps of red yarn, were getting the heavy tackles ready for the whales. But they worked rather slowly and talked very fast, and seemed in anything but a good humor. All their noses projected upward from their faces like so many bowsprits. Now and then pairs of them would drop their work and run up to the masthead to get some fresh air. Some, thinking they would catch the plague, dipped oakum in coal-tar and at intervals held it to their nostrils. Others, having broken the stems of their pipes almost short off at the bowl, were vigorously puffing tobacco smoke so that it constantly filled their nostrils.

Stubb was struck by a shower of outcries and curses coming from the captain's cabin aft. Looking in that direction, he saw a fiery face thrust from behind the door, which was held slightly open from within. This was the tormented surgeon, who after in vain protesting against the day's proceedings, had retreated to the captain's cabin to avoid the stench — but still could not help yelling out his pleas and objections from time to time.

Noting all this, Stubb saw his opportunity. Turning to the Guernseyman, he had a little chat with him, during which the mate expressed his contempt for his captain as a conceited fool who had brought them all into so stinking and unprofitable a mess. Sounding him carefully, Stubb further perceived that the Guernseyman had not the slightest suspicion concerning the ambergris. He therefore kept quiet on that subject, but otherwise was quite frank and friendly with him, so that the two quickly hatched a little plan for both outwitting and mocking the captain, without his at all suspecting their true intentions. According to this plan, the Guernseyman, under cover of being an interpreter, was to tell the captain whatever he pleased, but as if it came from Stubb. And as for Stubb, he was to utter whatever nonsense came to mind during the interview.

By this time their intended victim appeared from his cabin. He was a small, dark, but rather delicate-looking man for a sea-captain, with large whiskers and mustache, and he wore a red cotton velvet vest with watch-seals at his side. To this gentleman, Stubb was now politely introduced by the Guernseyman, who at once ostentatiously put on the manner of interpreting between them.
"What shall I say to him first?" said he.
"Why," said Stubb, eyeing the velvet vest and the watch and seals, "you may as well begin by telling him that he looks sort of babyish to me, though I don't pretend to be a judge."

"He says, Monsieur," said the Guernseyman in French, turning to his captain, "that only yesterday his ship spoke a vessel whose captain and chief mate, with six sailors, had all died of a fever caught from a blasted whale they had brought alongside."
Upon this the captain started, and eagerly wanted to know more.
"What now?" said the Guernseyman to Stubb.
"Why, since he takes it so easily, tell him that now I've eyed him carefully, I'm quite certain that he's no more fit to command a whale-ship than a monkey. In fact, tell him from me he's a baboon."
"He vows and declares, Monsieur, that the other whale, the dried one, is far more deadly than the blasted one. In short, Monsieur, he begs us, as we value our lives, to cut loose from these fish."
Instantly the captain ran forward, and in a loud voice commanded his crew to stop hoisting the cutting-tackles and at once cast loose the cables and chains confining the whales to the ship.
"What now?" said the Guernseyman, when the captain had returned to them.
"Why, let me see. Yes, you may as well tell him now that — that — in fact, tell him I've tricked him, and" — aside to himself — "perhaps somebody else."
"He says, Monsieur, that he's very happy to have been of any service to us."
Hearing this, the captain declared that they were the grateful parties — meaning himself and the mate — and concluded by inviting Stubb down to his cabin to drink a bottle of Bordeaux.
"He wants you to take a glass of wine with him," said the interpreter.
"Thank him heartily, but tell him it's against my principles to drink with the man I've tricked. In fact, tell him I must go."

"He says, Monsieur, that his principles won't admit of his drinking. But that if Monsieur wants to live another day to drink, then Monsieur had best drop all four boats and pull the ship away from these whales, for it's so calm they won't drift."

By this time Stubb was over the side, and getting into his boat, he hailed the Guernseyman to this effect: that having a long tow-line in his boat, he would do what he could to help them by pulling out the lighter whale from the ship's side. While the Frenchman's boats were engaged in towing the ship one way, Stubb benevolently towed his whale the other way, ostentatiously letting out an unusually long tow-line.

Presently a breeze sprang up. Stubb pretended to cast off from the whale. Hoisting his boats, the Frenchman soon increased his distance, while the Pequod slid in between him and Stubb's whale. Whereupon Stubb quickly pulled to the floating body, and hailing the Pequod to give notice of his intentions, at once proceeded to reap the fruit of his cunning trick. Seizing his sharp boat-spade, he commenced an excavation in the body, a little behind the side fin. You would almost have thought he was digging a cellar there in the sea. And when at length his spade struck against the gaunt ribs, it was like turning up old Roman tiles and pottery buried in rich English soil. His boat's crew were all in high excitement, eagerly helping their chief and looking as anxious as gold-hunters.

And all the time numberless birds were diving, ducking, screaming, yelling, and fighting around them. Stubb was beginning to look disappointed, especially as the horrible stench increased, when suddenly from out the very heart of this plague there stole a faint stream of perfume. It flowed through the tide of bad smells without being absorbed by it, as one river will flow into and along with another without at all blending with it for a time.
"I have it! I have it!" cried Stubb with delight, striking something in the underground regions. "A purse! A purse!"

Dropping his spade, he thrust both hands in and drew out handfuls of something that looked like ripe Windsor soap, or rich mottled old cheese — very oily and fragrant. You might easily dent it with your thumb. It is of a hue between yellow and ash-gray. And this, good friends, is ambergris, worth a gold guinea an ounce to any druggist. Some six handfuls were obtained. But more was unavoidably lost in the sea, and still more might have been secured were it not for impatient Ahab's loud command to Stubb to stop and come on board, else the ship would bid them goodbye.
